items.readable_text:
Content:
When we transform a logarithmic function [MATH: y = \log_a (x),] its domain might be modified as well.

Content:
For example, the diagram below shows the graph of the transformed logarithmic function [MATH: f(x) = \log_2(x-1).] What is the domain of [MATH: f(x)?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1b2655341e0798fee369b17aa1fbd9f6]

Content:
First, recall that the domain of [MATH: y=\log_a (x)] is
[MATH: x > 0.]

Content:
To find the domain of [MATH: f(x),] we take the above inequality and replace [MATH: x] with the argument (or input) of the logarithm function contained in [MATH: f(x).] In this case, the argument is [MATH: x-1,] so we get
[MATH: x-1 > 0.]

Content:
Solving this inequality, we obtain
[MATH: x − 1|> 0; x|> 1.]

Content:
Therefore, the domain of [MATH: y=f(x)] is [MATH: x\in(1, \infty).]

sections.normalized_html: What is the domain of [MATH: f(x)=\ln (2x+4)-2?]
sections.readable_text: What is the domain of [MATH: f(x)=\ln (2x+4)-2?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The domain of [MATH: y = \ln x] is [MATH: x \gt 0.]

To find the domain of [MATH: f(x),] we replace [MATH: x] with [MATH: 2x+4] in the above inequality. This gives [MATH: 2x+4 > 0.]

Solving this inequality, we obtain [MATH: 2x + 4|> 0; 2x|> − 4; x|> − 2.]

Therefore, the domain of [MATH: y = f(x)] is [MATH: x\in\left( -2, \infty \right).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

[MATH: x > 0.]

[MATH: x − 1|> 0; x|> 1.]

Therefore, the domain of [MATH: y=f(x)] is [MATH: x\in(1, \infty).]
